**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 30, verses 6–7:**

﴿Wa'da Allah﴾ is an emphatic infinitive (*masdar mu'akkid*), like your saying, "I owe you a thousand dirhams, *'urfan*" (acknowledged), because its meaning is: "I acknowledge it to you with an acknowledgment." And "the promise of Allah" is that He has promised it as a promise, because what precedes it has the sense of promising. Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, condemned them for being intelligent in worldly affairs, let alone in matters of religion, because they were people of trade and profit. This is also related from al-Hasan.

So skilled was one of them that he would take a dirham and tap it with his finger, and thereby know whether it was bad or good. His saying ﴿they know﴾ (*ya'lamun*) is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for his saying ﴿they do not know﴾ (*la ya'lamun*). In this substitution there is a subtle point: he substituted it for the first and placed it in a position where it stands in its place and fills its role, to make you aware that there is no difference between the absence of knowledge, which is ignorance, and the presence of a knowledge that does not go beyond this world. His saying ﴿an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾ indicates that the world has an outward and an inward aspect. Its outward aspect is what the ignorant know: enjoyment of its adornments and indulgence in its pleasures. Its inward aspect and reality is that it is a passage to the Hereafter, one provisions oneself from it for the Hereafter with obedience and righteous deeds. In the indefiniteness of ﴿an outward aspect﴾ there is: that they know only one outward aspect out of the whole range of outward aspects.

The second ﴿they﴾ (*hum*) may be a subject (*mubtada'*), with ﴿heedless﴾ (*ghafilun*) as its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of the first ﴿they﴾; or it may be a repetition of the first, with ﴿heedless﴾ as the predicate of the first. Whichever it is, its mention indicates that they are the very source of heedlessness of the Hereafter, its abode and its teacher, and that it springs from them and returns to them.

Among themselves. It is possible that this is an adverbial (ẓarf), as if it were said: "Have they not reflected within themselves," that is, in their hearts, which are empty of thought. Reflection occurs only in the hearts, but this is added as an amplified depiction of the state of those who reflect, as in your saying: "Believe it in your heart, and conceal it in your self (nafs)." It is also possible that it is a complement (ṣila) of the reflection, as in your saying: "He reflected upon the matter and turned his thought over it."

Mā khalaqa is connected to a deleted verb of saying, meaning: "Have they not reflected and then said this statement?" It has also been said that the meaning is: "that they might know," because the context contains an indication of it.

Except with truth and for a specified term: that is, He did not create them as vanity and sport, without a correct purpose and a far-reaching wisdom, nor to remain eternal. Rather, He created them joined to truth, accompanied by wisdom, and with a specified term appointed for them, to which they must inevitably come, namely the establishment of the Hour and the time of reckoning, reward and punishment. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did you then suppose that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ How He named their leaving unreturned to Him "vain."

The bāʾ in His saying "except with truth" is like it in your saying: "I entered upon him in travelling clothes," and "He bought the horse with its saddle and bridle," meaning: he bought it while it was equipped with the saddle and bridle, not separated from them. Likewise the meaning is: He did not create them except while they were conjoined with truth and attached to it. If you ask: when you make "in themselves" a complement of the reflection, what is its meaning? I say: its meaning is: "Have they not reflected upon their own selves, which are closer to them than other created things, and they know and are more informed about their states than they are about the states of anything else? Then let them ponder what God has deposited in them, outwardly and inwardly, of wondrous wisdoms indicating governance rather than neglect, and that they must inevitably reach a time at which the Judge who arranged their affair will repay them: good with good, and evil with its like. Then, at that time, they will know that the rest of creation is likewise ordered by wisdom and governance, and that they must reach that time." What is meant by "the meeting with their Lord" is the specified term.

Have they not travelled through the land and looked at the ends of those who came before them? They were greater than these in strength, and they ploughed the earth and cultivated it more than these have cultivated it. (Surah al-Rum 30:9)

This is an affirmation of their travelling in the lands and their looking at the traces of the destroyed nations, such as ʿAd, Thamud and others of the defiant peoples. Then He began describing their conditions to them, and that they were stronger than these, and that they stirred up the earth and tilled it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿You have a beast that is not broken to plough the earth﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah 2:71). It was also said that the cow used for tillage is called al-muthirah. And they said: the bull was named thawr because of its stirring up the earth, and the cow (baqarah) because it cleaves (tabqaruha) the earth, i.e., splits it. "And they cultivated it more than these have cultivated it": that is, those destroyed peoples cultivated it more than the cultivation of the people of Makkah. The people of Makkah are the people of a valley without crops; they have no stirring up of the earth at all, nor any cultivation of it whatsoever. So this is nothing but a mockery of them and a mention of the weakness of their condition in their worldly life, because the greater part of what the people of the world rely upon and boast of is the matter of agriculture (al-dahqanah) [[His words "amr al-dahqanah" mean agriculture (ʿ)]], and they too are weak in strength. So His words "they were greater than these in strength" means ʿAd, Thamud and their likes are of this kind, like His words: ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created them, is greater than them in strength?﴾ (Surah Fussilat 41:15), although this is more eloquent, because He is the creator of strength and power. Their destruction by Him was therefore not an injustice to them, since His condition is incompatible with injustice; rather, they wronged themselves in that they did what necessitated their destruction.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 30, verse 10:

It is read as ʿāqibatu in both the accusative and the nominative. As-Sūʾā is the feminine form of al-Asways (the worse), which is al-Aqbaḥ (the uglier), just as al-Ḥusnā is the feminine of al-Aḥsan (the better). The meaning is: they were punished in this world with destruction, and then their end was a worse one. However, the apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun; that is, the punishment which is the worst of punishments in the Hereafter, namely Hell, which was prepared for the disbelievers. And an-anna kadhdhabū means li-anna kadhdhabū (because they denied). It is also permissible for an-anna to mean ay (that/namely), since when the explanation of the evil deed is denial and mockery, it carries the sense of speech, as in nādā (he called out), kataba (he wrote), and what is similar to them. Another interpretation is that asāʾū as-sūʾā means iqtarafū al-khaṭīʾa allatī hiya aswaʾu al-khaṭāyā (they committed the sin which is the worst of sins), and an-anna kadhdhabū is an appositive explanation of it, and the predicate of kāna is omitted, as the answer of lammā and law is omitted, for the sake of intentional vagueness.
Then to Him you will be returned. That is, to His reward and His punishment. It is read with the "ta" (تاء, the letter ت, addressing the audience) and with the "ya" (ياء, the letter ي, third person).

It is said: "I debated with him and he was silenced (fa-ablas)," when he did not speak (qawluhu "idha lam yanbis" means he did not speak; this is the explanation given in al-Sihah). And he despaired of being able to argue. From this comes the expression "the she-camel that is mublās," meaning one that does not make a sound.

It is also read as yublis, with a fatha on the lam, from ablasahu, meaning he silenced him.

﴿And on the Day the Hour is established, the criminals will despair.﴾

﴿And they will have no intercessors from among their associates, and they will be disbelievers in their associates.﴾ That is, from among those they worshipped besides Allah. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 30, verses 17–19:

When He mentioned the promise and the threat, He followed it with mention of that which leads to the promise and saves from the threat. What is meant by "tasbih" (glorification) in its apparent sense is the declaring of God free from every imperfection and praising Him with what is good at these times, for the blessing of God that is manifest is renewed in them. It has also been said that it means prayer (salah). It was said to Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father: "Do you find the five prayers in the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes," and he recited this verse: ﴿When you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ — the evening prayers being the maghrib and the 'isha', ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾ the dawn prayer, ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾ the 'asr prayer, ﴿and when you enter the noon﴾ the zuhr prayer.

His saying ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾ is connected to his saying ﴿when you enter the evening﴾, and his saying ﴿and to Him belongs all praise in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a parenthetical clause between them. Its meaning: it is incumbent upon all discerning beings among the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth to praise Him.

If you say: why did al-Hasan, may God have mercy on him, hold that this verse is Medinan? I say: because he used to say, "The five prayers were made obligatory in Medina, and what was obligatory in Mecca was two units of prayer at no fixed time." The more widely held view, however, is that the five were made obligatory in Mecca. It is related from A'isha, may God be pleased with her: "Prayer was made obligatory as two units [[Agreed upon from the hadith of A'isha; the wording is that of Ahmad, and its context is more complete]], then when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) arrived in Medina, the prayer of travel was kept, and it was increased for the prayer of residence." It is related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever would like to be measured out for with the fullest measure, let him say: ﴿So glory be to God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning…﴾ — the verse [[Recorded by al-Tha'labi from the hadith of Anas, and in its chain is Bishr ibn al-Husayn, who is discarded (saqit)]]." And from him, peace be upon him: "Whoever says upon waking, ﴿So glory be to God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ — up to his saying ﴿and thus you will be brought forth﴾ — will attain what he missed in his day. And whoever says it when he enters the evening will attain what he missed in his night [[Recorded by Abu Dawud, al-'Uqayli and Ibn 'Adi from the hadith of Ibn Abbas. Its chain is weak, and al-Bukhari said: it is not sound]]."

In the reading of 'Ikrimah: ﴿hīnan tumsūna wa-hīnan tuṣbihūn﴾ (at times when you enter the evening and at times when you enter the morning). The meaning: you enter the evening in it and you enter the morning in it, like His saying ﴿a day on which no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾, meaning "in which."

﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾: the bird out of the egg; and ﴿the dead out of the living﴾: the egg out of the bird. The revival of the earth is the bringing forth of plants from it. ﴿And thus you will be brought forth﴾: like that bringing forth, you will be brought out of the graves and resurrected. The meaning: the beginning and the return are equal in the power of the One who is able to effect the reversal, namely bringing the dead out of the living and the living out of the dead, reviving the dead and causing the living to die. It was also read: ﴿al-Mayyit﴾ with shaddah [[His saying "and it was read al-Mayyit with shaddah" indicates that the well-known reading is with takhfif (lightening). (ʿAyn)]], and ﴿tukhrajūna﴾ with a fatha on the ta'.

Among His signs is that He created you from dust, since He created your origin from it. The particle "idha" here denotes sudden occurrence (lil-mufajaʼa), and its sense is: then, at the time of your existence as human beings dispersed upon the earth, you were suddenly [there], like His words: "And He spread from both of them many men and women."

"And from yourselves He created mates (azwaj)" because Hawwa' (Eve) was created from the rib of Adam, peace be upon him, and the women after her were created from the loins of men. Or [it means] from the form of yourselves and their kind, not from another kind; this is because between two of one kind there is affinity (al-alf) and tranquility (al-sukun), whereas between two differing kinds there is repulsion (al-tanafur). "And He placed between you affection (mawaddah) and mercy (rahmah)" through the protection of marriage, after there had been no prior acquaintance between you, no meeting, and no cause requiring compassion such as kinship or blood relation.

It is related from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, that "mawaddah" is a metaphor for intercourse and "rahmah" for offspring, as He said: "and a mercy from Us," and He said: "a mention of the mercy of your Lord toward His servant." It is said: "sakana ilayhi" means he inclined toward him, as in their saying "inqata'a ilayhi" and "itma'anna ilayhi"; and from it comes "al-sakan," which is the beloved one to whom one inclines, on the pattern of fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. Al-Alsina (ألسنة): languages. Or it means kinds of speech and their forms. Allah, Mighty and Exalted, varied these things so that you can hardly hear two speakers who agree in softness or loudness, in harshness or gentleness, in eloquence or accent (lukna), in arrangement or style, nor in any other of the qualities and conditions of speech. Likewise with forms and their outlines, and colours and their varieties. Because of this variation, recognition (ta'aruf) takes place; otherwise, if they were alike, similar and of one kind, there would be confusion and ambiguity, many benefits would be lost, and you might see twins who resemble each other in appearance, so that you are mistaken in distinguishing between them. You thus come to know the wisdom of Allah in the variation of appearances. In this is a clear sign, since they were born of one father and branched from a single origin, yet they are, in their great number, which only Allah knows, different and diverse.

It is also read as lil-'alimin (لِلْعَالِمِينَ) with a fatha and with a kasra on the lam. The reading with kasra is supported by His saying, ﴿وَمَا يَعْقِلُهَا إِلَّا الْعَالِمُونَ﴾ ("And none understand them except those who have knowledge").

Time and what occurs in it are like one thing, with the laff helping towards unity. It is also permissible that what is meant is: your sleeping in both times, and your seeking in both of them. The apparent meaning is the first, because it recurs in the Qur'an, and the most correct of meanings is what the Qur'an indicates, [heard] by attentive ears.

**Translation:**

In *yurīkum* (يُرِيكُمُ) there are two possibilities: an implied (verb) and treating the verb as if it were a verbal noun (maṣdar). The proverb is explained in both ways: *"Tasmaʿu bi-l-muʿaydi khayrun min an tarāhu"* ("Hearing of al-Muʿaydi is better than seeing him"). Also the saying of the poet:

*"They said, 'What would you like?' I said, 'I would amuse myself until morning, the first of all that is preferred.'*
*I stayed awake, with my companions in the narrow Ghamq, for a far-spreading lightning from Tihama.*
*They gave me wine to drink, then they surrounded me, enemies of God because of their lies and falsehood.*
*They said, 'What would you like?' I said, 'I would amuse myself until morning, the first of all that is preferred.'"*

This is by ʿUrwa ibn al-Ward al-ʿAbsī. *Arraqtu* (أرقت) means I stayed awake. The *wāw* in *wa-ṣuḥbatī* is for accompaniment (*wāw al-maʿiyya*). *Al-Mudayyaq* means the narrow place. *ʿAmq*, with a kasra and then a sukūn, is a kind of tree in the lands of the Ḥijāz; with a ḍamma and then a fatḥa, it is a low-lying place near Mecca. He may have made it quiescent here for the metre. *Li-barq* is connected to *arraqtu*: I stayed awake in this place because of a lightning from Tihama in the direction of my beloved. It is possible that the *wāw* is circumstantial (*ḥāliyya*), and *ṣuḥbatī* is the subject, with *bi-maḍīq ʿamq* as its predicate. If his companions were in it, then he was in it too, and this returns to the first reading. *Mustaṭīr* means spreading out. It is also narrated as *saqūnī al-nasīʾ* (they gave me *nasīʾ*). *Nasaʾtu al-laban* means I mixed milk with water, so *al-nasīʾ* is milk mixed with water. *Takanfūnī* means they surrounded me. *ʿAdāt* is the plural of *ʿādin*, meaning *ʿadūw* (enemy).

It is also said that it is the plural of *ʿadūw*, meaning they are enemies of God because of their lies and falsehood, and this is a parenthetical clause (*jumla iʿtirāḍiyya*). It is possible that *ʿadāt* is an apposition (*badal*) from the pronoun of the subject, or a subject according to the dialect of one who says *akalūnī al-barāghīth* (the fleas ate me). That is, they surrounded me and said, "What do you want?" I said, "*Alhū*" (I would amuse myself), meaning that it is my amusing myself. Here *an* is implied in meaning, even though the verb is not in the subjunctive in form. Al-Jawharī said: one says *ifʿal hādhā āthara dhī athīr*, meaning "the first of every thing." This indicates that *āthar* is in the accusative as a figurative adverb of place (*ẓarf majāzī*) or circumstantial (*ḥāl*). That is, do it while it is the first of everything that is preferred. So it is a superlative (*afʿal al-tafḍīl*) in the sense of the passive participle. Ibn al-Ḥājib stated that this is permissible and that it occurs rarely. *Athara* with a short or a long *hamza* means that he preferred it over others. *Athīr* is a passive participle in the sense of *maʾthūr* (transmitted or preferred). Or it means "deserving of precedence." So the meaning is: the first of everything is the owner of something preferred, and so he is the preferred and foremost one. Or the sense is: my amusement throughout the night is the foremost thing for me.

*Khawfan min al-ṣāʿiqa aw min al-ikhlāf* (out of fear of the thunderbolt or of failure of rain), *wa-ṭamaʿan fī al-ghayth* (and in hope of rain). It is said: *khawfan* for the traveller and *ṭamaʿan* for the one who is present. Both are in the accusative as an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*, i.e., the accusative of cause or reason). If you say: it is required that the object of purpose be the action of the subject of the verb being explained, and fear and hope are not like that. I answer: there are two possible answers. The first is that the two objects are in meaning the subjects, because they are seeing, so it is as if it were said: He makes you see the lightning, fearing and hoping. The second is that it is by deleting a noun that is modified: the meaning is "the desire of fear and the desire of hope," so the modified noun is deleted and the noun it is attached to takes its place. It is also permissible that both are circumstantial (*ḥāl*), meaning fearful and hopeful. *Yunazzilu* was also read with the intensive form (*tashdīd*).

[[Mahmud said: If you say, "Why is *khawfan* and *ṭamaʿan* in the accusative as objects of purpose while they are not the actions of the subject of the verb being explained, what is the explanation?" I answer: the objects here are the subjects, because they are seeing. So the meaning is: He makes you see the lightning, fearing and hoping. Or by deletion of a modified noun, the meaning is: the desire of your fear and your hope.]]

Ahmad said: Fear and hope are among the created things of God the Exalted and signs of His power. In that case the conditions for the accusative apply to both of them: they are verbal nouns and they exist together at the same time. The creator is one, so it is necessary to point out an interpretation of the accusative other than this one. We say: the grammarians' statement about the object of purpose, that it must be the action of the subject, means that the subject must be characterised by it. An example: if you say, "I came to you out of honour for you," you have described yourself as honouring, and you are saying in meaning, "I came to you honouring you." **Al-Zamakhshari** (*al-Kashshaf*): "If you say: what is the difference between the first, the second and the third [prepositions] in His saying ﴿from yourselves﴾, ﴿from what your right hands possess﴾, ﴿among partners﴾?" I say: the first, *min* (مِنْ), is for the starting point, as if He said: He took a parable from something of yourselves, namely your own selves, and drew it from what is closest, and it was not far. The second, *min* (مِنْ), is partitive (*lil-tab'id*). The third, *min* (مِنْ), is superfluous, added to reinforce the interrogation that functions as a negation. Its meaning is: Do you accept for yourselves, and for your slaves who are like you, humans like humans and slaves like slaves, that some of them should share with you in what We have provided you of wealth and other things, so that you and they are equal in it, without any distinction between free and slave? Do you fear to act arbitrarily without them, and to encroach upon them in managing it, as some of you free men fear each other? If you do not accept this for yourselves, how then do you accept for the Lord of lords and the Owner of the free and the slaves that you make some of His slaves partners with Him? ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like this detailed explanation, ﴿We detail the signs﴾, that is, We make them clear, because the parable reveals meanings and makes them plain, since it is like depicting and shaping them.

Do you not see how He depicted *shirk* (associating partners with God) in a distorted image?

Those who did wrong, i.e. associated partners with God, like His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Indeed, association [with God] is a great wrong﴾ [Qur'an 31:13]. Without knowledge: i.e. they followed their desires while ignorant, because the one who knows, when he mounts his desire, is sometimes restrained and held back by his knowledge. As for the ignorant, he wanders aimlessly like an animal, and nothing restrains him. ﴿Whom God leaves astray﴾: i.e. whom He forsakes and does not show kindness (luṭf) to, knowing that he is one for whom there is no kindness, so who could guide the like of him? His saying ﴿and they will have no helpers﴾ is evidence that the meaning of "leaving astray" is forsaking.

[[His saying "whom God leaves astray: whom He forsakes" — interpreting leaving astray in this way is based on the premise that God does not create evil, which is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. The People of the Sunna held that He creates evil just as He creates good, so the verse is to be taken at face value. (Ṭ)]]

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 30, verses 30–32:**

﴿So set your face toward the religion﴾: that is, make your face upright and straight toward it, and keep it aligned, not turning aside to the right or to the left. This is a metaphor for facing the religion, standing firm upon it, persevering in it, and being concerned with its means. For whoever is concerned with something fixes his gaze upon it, directs his sight toward it, and straightens his face to face it. ﴿Hanifan﴾ (upright, inclining away from falsehood) is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the one addressed, or of ﴿the religion﴾. ﴿Fitrata Allah﴾ means: adhere to the fitrah (innate nature) of God, or: upon you is the fitrah of God. I have supposed it (the verb) to be addressed in the plural because of His words ﴿turning penitently to Him﴾. ﴿Munībīna﴾ (turning penitently) is a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "adhere". His words ﴿and fear Him, establish prayer, and do not be among the polytheists﴾ are conjoined to this implied pronoun. The fitrah is the created nature. Do you not see His words ﴿there is no changing of God's creation﴾? The meaning is that He created them disposed to monotheism and the religion of Islam, not turning away from it nor denying it, because it answers the intellect and accords with sound reasoning, such that, had they been left alone, they would have chosen no other religion. Whoever among them went astray did so through the seduction of the devils of mankind and jinn. From this is his (ﷺ) saying: "Every servant of Mine I have created upright (ḥunafā'), but the devils led them astray from their religion and commanded them to associate with Me what I have not sanctioned." [[His words "fajtālatahumu al-shayāṭīn" mean: the devils turned them around. This is what the Ṣiḥāḥ (Lexicon) conveys. (ʿ)]] [[Muslim transmitted it from the hadith of ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār, and more complete than this.]] And his (ﷺ) saying, peace be upon him: "Every child is born upon the fitrah, until his parents make him a Jew or a Christian." [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah.]] ﴿There is no changing of God's creation﴾: that is, it is not fitting that this fitrah be altered or changed.

If you ask: why was the address first in the singular and then in the plural? I answer: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was addressed first, and addressing the Messenger is addressing his community, along with what it contains of honoring the leader. Then the plural was used afterward for clarification and summary.

﴿Of those who divided their religion﴾ is a substitute for ﴿the polytheists﴾: they abandoned the religion of Islam. It is also read ﴿farraqū﴾ with the doubled letter, meaning they made it into many religions according to the divergence of their desires. ﴿And became sects﴾: factions, each one following the leader who misled it. ﴿Every faction, rejoicing in what is with them﴾: each party is pleased with its doctrine, thinking its falsehood to be truth. It is also permissible that ﴿of those who﴾ be disconnected from what precedes it, its meaning being: among those who separate from their religion, every faction is rejoicing in what they have. But ﴿farihūn﴾ (rejoicing) has been put in the nominative as a description of ﴿kull﴾ (every), as in the verse:

*"Every friend who does not humble himself... is deserving of being shunned and turned away from, not of affection."*

This is by al-Shammākh. Another transmission gives, in place of the second half-line: *"by the cutting off of a resolute friend or one who forsakes him."* And "ghayr hāḍim" (not humbling himself), in the nominative, is a description of ﴿kull﴾; or in the genitive, a description of ﴿khalīl﴾ (friend), meaning: whoever does not lower himself to his companion is deserving of being shunned and turned away from, not of love. The fāʾ (then) was added because the subject contains the meaning of a condition. Ṣārim means "severing", and muṣādir means "avoiding": whoever does not lower himself to maintain his friend's union, which leads him to severance; and if not severance, then avoidance. So it is as if he has severed, or avoided in fact.

The lam in لِيَكْفُرُوا is figurative (majaz), like the lam in لِيَكُونَ لَهُمْ عَدُوًّا. فَتَمَتَّعُوا is parallel to اعْمَلُوا ما شِئْتُمْ فَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ, and [the meaning is] "the consequence of your enjoyment" (wabal tamattu'ikum). Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) read it as وليتمتعوا.

Ad-darr (al-darr): hardship, whether from emaciation, sickness, drought, or something else. Al-rahmah: deliverance from hardship.

The lam in لِيَكْفُرُوا is figurative (majaz), like the lam in لِيَكُونَ لَهُمْ عَدُوًّا. فَتَمَتَّعُوا is parallel to اعْمَلُوا ما شِئْتُمْ فَسَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ, and [the meaning is] "the consequence of your enjoyment" (wabal tamattu'ikum). Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) read it as وليتمتعوا.

Al-sultan: the proof (ḥujjah), and "speaks" it. This is a metaphor, as you say: "his book speaks of such-and-such," and this is among the things the Qur'an has spoken of.

Its meaning: the indication and the testimony, as if he said: "so it bears witness to their shirk and to its soundness." The "mā" in "bimā kānū yushrikūn" is a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle, meaning: "by their being associates to God." It is permissible for it to be a relative (mawṣūlah) particle, with the pronoun returning to it, and its meaning would be: "so it speaks of the matter which they are causing to associate." It may also be that the meaning is: "Or have We sent down to them one who has authority (sulṭān), that is, a king with him a proof, so that king speaks of the proof by which they associate."

When We let people taste mercy, meaning a blessing such as rain, abundance or health, they rejoice in it; but if an evil afflicts them, meaning a calamity such as drought, hardship or sickness, and its cause is the ill omen of their sins, they despair of mercy.

Then He rebukes them, saying that they already know that He is the One who extends and withholds provision. So why do they despair of His mercy? And why do they not turn back to Him in repentance from the sins for which they were punished with hardship, so that He might restore His mercy to them?

The right of the near relative: the maintaining of family ties (silat al-rahim). And the right of the needy and the wayfarer: their share of the charity designated for them.

Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, cited this verse as evidence for the obligation of maintenance (nafaqah) for one's unmarriageable relatives (mahram) when they are needy and unable to earn a living. According to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, maintenance on the basis of kinship is owed only to children and parents. He analogized all other kinship relations to that of a paternal cousin (ibn al-amm), because there is no offspring relation between them.

If you ask: how is His saying, ﴿So give to the near relative﴾, connected to what precedes it, such that the particle fa' (so) is used? I answer: when He mentioned that the evil had befallen them because of what their hands had sent forward, He followed it with mention of what must be done and what must be avoided. ﴿Those who desire the Face of Allah﴾: the word "face" (wajh) may be understood to mean His essence, or His direction and side; that is, they intend by their good deed Him alone, sincerely, and His right, as in His saying, ﴿except seeking the Face of their Lord, the Most High﴾. Or it means they aim at the direction of drawing near to Allah and no other direction. The two meanings are close, but the manner of expression differs.

This verse has the same meaning as God's words (Exalted is He): "God destroys usury (riba) and makes charity (sadaqat) grow." The sense is: "And whatever you give of riba to the devourers of riba, so that it may increase (li-yarbuwa) in their wealth, i.e., so that it may grow and multiply in their possessions, it does not grow with God and is not blessed. And whatever zakah you give, i.e., charity by which you seek His Face sincerely, not seeking in return any recompense or show and reputation, then those are the ones who receive multiplication (al-mudh'ifun), those who have multiplied good deeds." The counterpart of al-mudh'if is al-muqwi (the one who has strength) and al-musir (the one who has wealth), for one who possesses strength and affluence. It has been recited with a fatha on the ʿayn (mudʿafun). It was also said: it was revealed concerning Thaqif, who used to practice riba. It was also said: the meaning is that a man gives a gift to another man or presents him with a gift, so that he will be compensated with more than what he gave or presented. That excess is not forbidden, but the one who compensates is not rewarded for that excess. They also said: riba is of two kinds. The forbidden kind is every loan in which more is taken than was given, or which draws a benefit. The kind that is not forbidden is that one seeks by his gift or present more than it. In a hadith: "The one who seeks a return on his gift is rewarded for it." [[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah and ʿAbd al-Razzaq by two routes, from Ibn Sirin, from Shurayh, as a statement of Shurayh (mawquf).]] It has also been recited: "wa-ma ataytum min riba," meaning: "and whatever you have encountered or incurred of giving riba." It has also been recited: "li-turbu," i.e., so that you may increase their wealth, like God's words "and He makes charity grow" (yurbi al-sadaqat), i.e., increases it. His words "then those are the ones who receive multiplication" (fa-ulaika hum al-mudh'ifun) are a fine shift (iltifat) in address, as if He said to His angels and His chosen creatures: "Those who seek the Face of God with their charities, they are the ones who receive multiplication." This is more praiseworthy for them than to say, "You are the ones who receive multiplication." The meaning is "those who are multiplied by it" (al-mudh'afun bihi), since there must be a pronoun referring back to "ma." Another possibility is that its implied construction is: "fa-mu'tuhu ulaika hum al-mudh'ifun" ("so those who give it, they are the ones who receive multiplication"). The omission is due to the evidence in the statement itself; this is the easier interpretation, while the first is richer in benefit.

Allah is the subject (mubtada'), and His predicate is "who created you" (alladhi khalaqakum), meaning: Allah is the one who does these specific acts, none of which anyone other than Him is able to do. Then He said, "Is there any of your partners (shurakā'ikum) — those you have taken as rivals to Him, whether idols or others — who does any one of those acts at all?" so that what you claim could be valid. Then He considered their condition to be far removed from the condition of their partners. It is also permissible for "who created you" (alladhi khalaqakum) to be a qualifier (ṣifah) of the subject, with the predicate being "is there any of your partners," and His saying "of that (min dhālikum)" is what links the clause to the subject, because its meaning is: "of His acts." As for "min" in the first, second and third instances, each of them is independently emphatic, to render their partners incapable and to show the ignorance of their worshippers.

Corruption has appeared on the land and the sea (fasad fi'l-barr wa'l-bahr). Examples: drought and famine, a decrease in the yield of crops, loss in trade, the outbreak of death among people and animals, the abundance of burnings and drownings, the failure of hunters and fishermen [[On his words "and the failure of hunters" (wa-ikhfaq al-sayyadin): in al-Sihah, akhfaqa al-sa'id means he returned without having hunted. (Ed.)]] and of those who seize (al-ghasa), the loss of blessing in everything, a general lack of benefit and abundance of harm. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas:

The land became barren and the source of the sea was cut off. They also said: when the rain ceases, the creatures of the sea go blind. And it is reported from al-Hasan that what is meant by "the sea" is the cities of the sea and its villages that lie on its shore. And it is reported from 'Ikrimah: the Arabs call the great cities "seas." It is also read as "wa'l-bihar" (fi'l-barr wa'l-bihar), with the plural form. "Because of what the hands of people have earned" (bima kasabat aydi al-nas): because of their disobedience and their sins, like the Almighty's saying: ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you, it is because of what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 30]. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿Corruption has appeared on the land﴾: by the killing of Adam's son his brother. And regarding "in the sea": that Julanda used to seize every ship by force. And it is reported from Qatadah: that was before the Prophet was sent (ba'th); then, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent, people returned, turning back from error and wrongdoing. It is also permissible that it means the appearance of evil and sins through the earning of people of that. If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿that He may let them taste some of what they have done, so that they may return﴾? I say: as for the first interpretation, it is clear, namely that God has corrupted the means of their worldly life and destroyed them, so that He makes them taste the consequence of some of their deeds in this world before He punishes them with all of them in the Hereafter, so that they may perhaps return from what they are upon. As for the second, the lam is figurative, in the sense that the appearance of evils through their agency is something for which they deserved that God make them taste the consequence of their deeds, in the desire that they return; so it is as if they only caused corruption and became the cause of the spreading of sins in the earth for that reason. It is also read "linudhiqahum" with the nun.

Then he emphasized that sins are the cause of God's wrath and retribution: He commanded them to travel through the earth and look at how God destroyed the nations and made them taste the evil consequence of their sins. And by His saying ﴿كانَ أَكْثَرُهُمْ مُشْرِكِينَ﴾ ("most of them were polytheists") He indicated that polytheism alone was not the cause of their destruction, and that what falls short of it, namely other sins, is also a cause of that.

Al-Qayyim: the upright, the most perfect in straightness, "in which there can be no crookedness." Min Allah (from Allah) may be connected with ya'ti (comes), so the meaning is: before there comes from Allah a Day that no one can turn back, as in His saying, ﴿So they will not be able to avert it﴾. Or it may be connected with mardd (that which can be turned back), in the sense: He Himself will not turn it back after He brings it, and there is no turning back of it on His part. Al-Maradd is a verbal noun meaning the act of turning back. ﴿Yasdda'un﴾ (yatasaddda'un): that is, they will split apart, scatter, as in His saying, ﴿And on the day the Hour is established, on that day they will be divided.﴾

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 30, verses 44–45:

﴿Whoever disbelieves, his disbelief is upon him﴾: a comprehensive expression covering every harm beyond which there is no further end, for whoever's harm is his disbelief, every kind of harm surrounds him.

﴿And for themselves they prepare (yamhadun)﴾: that is, they arrange for themselves what one arranges for oneself, the one who spreads out his bed and makes it smooth, so that nothing in his resting place disturbs him, nothing that keeps him awake or spoils his sleep: such as a protrusion or pebbles [[On his words "such as a protrusion or pebbles": al-natw means a raised part, and al-qadad means small pebbles. Reported by al-Sihah. (ʿ)]] or anything else that disturbs the sleeper. It is also permissible that it means: "so for themselves they prepare (for the Hereafter)," from the saying about one who prepares for himself: "He spread a bed for him and made him sleep." The placing of the adverbial phrase in both places indicates that the harm of disbelief returns only upon the disbeliever and does not pass beyond him, and that the benefit of faith and righteous deeds returns only to the believer and does not go beyond him.

﴿That He may reward out of His bounty those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: the particle li (so that) is connected to yamhadun and gives its reason. ﴿Out of His bounty﴾: [He adds] to them, beyond the fulfilment of what is due in reward. This resembles a metonymy (kinayah), because bounty follows reward, so it can only occur after what it follows has taken place. Or it means: out of His gift, which is His reward, because in the Arabic usage al-fudul and al-fawadil are gifts.

The repetition of ﴿those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾, and the use of the explicit noun in place of a pronoun, establish that none succeeds in His sight except the believing righteous. His saying ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾ is a confirmation following a confirmation, by way of contrast and by way of its converse.

The winds (al-riyah) are the south, the north and the eastern wind (al-saba), and these are winds of mercy. As for the dabur (the western wind), it is a wind of punishment.

From this is his (ﷺ) saying: "O Allah, make them winds (riyahan) and do not make them a wind (ريحا) [[Narrated by al-Shafi'i: "Akhbarani man la uttahamu (one whom I do not suspect) on the authority of al-'Ala' ibn Rashid, on the authority of 'Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, as a marfu' report similar to it," and by his chain he narrated it in al-Ma'rifah and in al-Da'awat. This unnamed narrator is Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya, who is weak. It has another route in Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani and Ibn 'Adi, through the narration of Husayn ibn Qays on the authority of 'Ikrimah, and Husayn is also weak.]]"

He (al-Zamakhshari) enumerated the purposes of their being sent: that He sent them to give good news of rain, and to make people taste mercy, which is the descent of rain and the fertility that follows it, the refreshment that comes with the blowing of the wind, and the purification of the land. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the overturned places (al-mu'tafikat) increase, the land is purified" [[I have not found it.]]; and the removal of corruption from the air, the winnowing of grains, and other things. And "that the ships may run (wa-litajriya al-fulk) in the sea" when they blow. He added "by His command" (bi-amrihi) because the wind may blow without being favourable (mu'atiyah), so there must be the anchoring of ships and the contrivance to hold them back, and sometimes it may storm and sink them. "And that you may seek of His bounty" (wa-litabtaghu min fadlihi), meaning the trade of the sea, "and that you may be thankful" (wa-litashkuru) for the blessing of Allah in it.

If you ask: to what does "wa-liyudhikakum" (and that He may make you taste) relate? I say: there are two opinions. It may be coordinated (ma'tuf) with "mubashshirat" (bringing good news) in meaning, as if it were said: "to bring you good news and to make you taste." Or it may relate to an omitted element whose estimate is: "wa-liyudhikakum, wa-liyakuna kadha wa-kadha: arsalnaha" (We sent them so that He may make you taste, and so that such-and-such may happen).

He shortened the way to the purpose by including, under the mention of victory and help, the mention of both groups, although he had first left the speech free of mention of them. And His saying ﴿It was ever a duty upon Us to help the believers﴾ is an exaltation of the believers, an elevation of their rank, a qualification for a noble honour, and a manifestation of the excellence of their precedence and distinction, in that He made them deserving, upon God, that He should help them, and made it binding upon Him that He should give them victory and make them triumph. It may be paused upon "qa" (ḥaqqan), and its meaning is: "And retribution against them was a truth." Then one begins: "lana naṣru al-mu'minīn."

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no Muslim man who defends the honour of his brother except that it is a truth upon God that He will ward off from him the Fire of Hell on the Day of Resurrection." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, Ahmad and al-Tabarani from the hadith of Abu al-Darda, and he said it is ḥasan (good). Ishaq, al-Tabarani, Abu Ya'la and Ibn 'Adi related it through the route of Shahr ibn Hawshab from Asma bint Yazid, raised to the Prophet, similar to it, and its isnad is weak. It was differed about regarding Shahr ibn Hawshab: al-'Ilaj related it from him in this way, while Layth ibn Abi Sulaym related it from him from Abu Hurayra. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it.]]

Then he recited His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It was ever a duty upon Us to help the believers﴾.

Then He spreads it out in the sky however He wills, sometimes continuous, and sometimes He makes it fragments (kisafan), that is, pieces. So you see the rain (al-wadq) coming out from within it, in both cases alike. By "the sky" is meant the heavens, which it splits and cleaves, as in His saying ﴿and its branches are in the sky﴾. And by "striking His servants" is meant striking their lands and their territories. ﴿from before it﴾ is by way of repetition and emphasis, as in His saying ﴿so the outcome of both of them is that they are in the Fire, abiding therein﴾. The purpose of the emphasis here is to show that their long wait for rain had been prolonged and extended, so their despair became firm and their despondency (iblasuhum) persisted [[His saying "iblasuhum": al-iblas (despair) is despair of good, silence, and being broken by grief and sorrow. Recorded in al-Sihah. (E)]], so their joy at the rain was in proportion to their distress over it.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿فَانظُرْ إِلَىٰ آثَارِ رَحْمَةِ اللَّهِ كَيْفَ يُحْيِي الْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا﴾ is not quoted here; the passage itself uses the verse's wording, so I render the quoted words as they stand.

Read as: "Athar" and "āthār" (the singular and plural forms), on the basis of unity and plurality. Abu Haywa and others read: "kayfa tuhyā" (how it gives life), meaning: the mercy.

Inna dhalika (indeed that), meaning: indeed that Capable One who gives life to the earth after its death is the One who gives life to people after their death, wa huwa ʿala kulli shayʾin qadir (and He is Capable of everything). This is among the things within the scope of His power, as shown by the act of bringing into being (al-insha').

Then they will see it: the trace of God's mercy. For God's mercy is the rain, and its trace is the vegetation. Whoever reads it in the plural (āthār), the pronoun refers back to its meaning, since the meaning of "traces of mercy" is vegetation, and the name of vegetation (nabāt) applies to both the little and the much, for it is a verbal noun used as a name for what grows.

As for "wa-la-in" (and indeed if): the lām is the lām of preparation (al-lām al-muwaṭṭi'ah) for an oath, which entered upon the conditional particle. "La-ẓallū" (they would surely remain) is the answer to the oath, and it stands in place of both answers, that is, the answer to the oath and the answer to the condition. The meaning is: they will surely remain, blaming God, saying that when He withholds rain from them they despair of His mercy and strike their chins upon their chests, dumbfounded; but when He lets them reach His mercy and provides them with rain, they rejoice and exult; and when He sends a wind that strikes their crops so that they turn yellow, they cry out and disbelieve in God's blessing. So in all of these states they are in the blameworthy condition: it was incumbent upon them to rely upon God and His bounty, but they despaired; and to be thankful for His blessing and praise Him for it, but they added nothing to their joy and exultation; and to be patient under His trial, but they disbelieved. The wind that makes the vegetation turn yellow may be a hot wind (ḥarūr) or a cold wind (ḥarjaf), for both of them are things that wither (yaṣūḥ) the vegetation and make it into dry stubble (hashīm). He said "muṣfarran" (yellowed) because that yellowness is newly arisen. It was also said: "They saw the cloud yellowed," because when it is like that it does not rain.

Recited with a fatha and with a damma on the ḍād (ḍaʿf and ḍuʿf), and these are two dialects, though the damma is stronger in recitation, based on what Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both) reported: he said, "I recited it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'min ḍuʿf,' and he taught me 'min ḍuʿf.'" [Narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ishaq and al-Bazzar from the hadith of ʿAṭiyya from Ibn ʿUmar, without the explanation. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it through Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ from Nafiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar, but its isnad contains Salam ibn Sulayman.]

His saying, ﴿Who created you from weakness﴾ is like His saying, ﴿Man was created of haste﴾. He means that the foundation of your affairs, what you are built upon, your physique and your constitution, is weakness. ﴿And man was created weak﴾: that is, We began bringing you into existence in weak states at the beginning. That is the condition of infancy and youth until you reached the time of puberty and vigor, and that is the condition of strength until maturity and reaching full strength. Then you were returned to your original state, which is weakness, through old age and decrepitude. It has been said: "from weakness" refers to the drops of semen, as in His saying, ﴿from a despised fluid﴾. This repetition across the different states, and the change from one form to another and from one attribute to another, is the clearest proof and the most just witness to the All-Knowing, All-Powerful Creator.

The Hour: the Resurrection (al-qiyamah). It is so called because it will occur at the last hour of the worldly life (al-dunya). Or because it will come upon them suddenly and unexpectedly (baghtatan wa-badihatan). As one says "in an hour" to someone whom you want to hurry; and it became a proper name for it, like "the star" (al-najm) for the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), and "the planet" (al-kawkab) for Venus (al-Zuhara).

And they meant: their stay (labthuhum) in the world, or in the graves, or in the interval between the end of the world and the Resurrection (al-ba'th). And in a hadith: "Between the end of the world and the time of the Resurrection is forty [[I have not found it in this form. In the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Between the two blasts is forty." They said: "O Abu Hurayrah, forty years?" He said: "I refuse." They said: "Forty months?" He said: "I refuse." They said: "Forty days?" He said: "I refuse."]]." They said: "We do not know whether it is forty years or forty thousand years." That is a time in which they will perish and their punishment will cease; and they estimate the duration of their stay by that, in a manner of considering it brief. Or they forget, or they lie, or they conjecture.

﴿Thus they were turned away﴾ (kadhalika kanu yu'fakun): that is, in the same manner of turning away they used to be turned away from truth and verification in the world; and likewise they used to base their affairs on opposition to the truth. Or, in the same manner of falsehood (al-ifk) they used to be deluded, in being deceived by what has now become clear to them: that it was only an hour.

The reciters (al-qa'ilun) are the angels, the prophets, and the believers. "In the Book of God" means in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh). Or it means in God's knowledge and decree. Or it means in what He wrote, i.e., what He made obligatory by His wisdom. They rejected what they had said and swore to it, and they informed them of the truth. Then they followed that with a rebuke for their denial of the Resurrection in their words: ﴿This is the Day of Resurrection, but you used not to know﴾ that it is true, because of your neglect in seeking the truth and following it.

If you ask: what is this fa' (فاء, "then") and what is its reality? I answer: it is the fa' in the line of verse:

﴿So we have come to Khurasan﴾ [[The explanation of this evidence was given earlier in this volume, page 271, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

Its reality is that it is the response to a condition implied by the speech, as if he said: if what you said is true, that Khurasan is the furthest place we are to be driven, then we have come to Khurasan, and it is time for us to be freed. Likewise, if you were deniers of the Resurrection, then this is the Day of Resurrection, meaning that the falsity of your claim has become clear.

Al-Hasan read ﴿yawm al-ba'th﴾ with the vowel on the middle letter (as yawmu al-ba‘th, i.e., with a sukun-less pronunciation of the ‘ayn-free form). ﴿Lā yanfa'u﴾ is read with the yā' and with the tā'. ﴿Yusta'tabūn﴾ comes from your saying: "istatabanī fulān, fa-a'tabtuhu," meaning: he asked me to be pleased, so I pleased him. That is when you have wronged him. The reality of a'tabtuhu is: I removed his blame (ʿatb). Do you not see his saying:

﴿Tamim became angry that ‘Amir should be killed, on the day of al-Nassar; so they were appeased by al-Sayhum﴾ [[The explanation of this evidence was given in the first volume, page 105, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]] How he made them angry, then said "fa-a'tabū," meaning: their anger was removed. Anger has the meaning of blame. The meaning is:

It is not said to them: "Please your Lord with repentance and obedience." Similar to this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will not be taken out of it, and they will not be asked to make amends﴾.

If you ask: how did they make them not asked to make amends in some verses and not blamed in others, since He says ﴿And if they ask to make amends, they will not be among those who are granted it﴾? I answer: as for their not being asked to make amends, this is its meaning. As for their not being blamed, its meaning is that they are not content with what they are in, so their condition is likened to the condition of a people who were wronged, and they are blaming the wrongdoer and not content with him. So if they ask God to make amends, that is, ask Him to remove what they are in, then they are not among those who are answered in its removal.

And We have certainly presented for them every description, each one so strange that it is like a parable, and related to them every story of wondrous import, such as the description of those raised up on the Day of Resurrection, their tale, what they will say, what will be said to them, and their excuses, which will not avail them, and their pleas for indulgence, which will not be heard. But they, because of the hardness of their hearts and their aversion to hearing the news of the Hereafter, when you bring them a sign from the verses of the Qur'an, say, "You have brought us only falsehood and nonsense." Then He said: "Thus does God seal the hearts of the ignorant." And the meaning of God's sealing is withholding the divine graces [[His saying "the meaning of God's sealing is withholding the divine graces" is an interpretation based on the premise that He, exalted is He, does not create evil, which is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah.

The People of the Sunnah held that He creates it just as He creates good, so the verse is to be taken at face value. (ʿ)]] by which hearts are expanded so that they accept the truth. He withholds them only from one whom He knows they will not benefit or avail, just as a preacher withholds an admonition from one who is clearly shown that the admonition is idle and will not take effect on him. This is therefore a metaphor for the hardness of their hearts and the rust and corrosion that have settled upon them. It is as if He said: thus do the hearts of the ignorant harden and rust, until they call the people of truth falsifiers, while they themselves are the most deeply rooted of God's creatures in that trait [[His saying "the most deeply rooted of God's creatures" — in the Sihah: "a'raqa al-rajul" means he became noble, i.e., one who has a root in nobility. (ʿ)]]. So be patient in the face of their enmity. Indeed, God's promise of your victory and the manifestation of your religion over all religions is true; it must certainly be fulfilled and honored. Let not their saying and doing bring you to lightness and anxiety through distress at what they say and do, for they are a people in doubt and astray, and such conduct from them is not to be wondered at. It is also read with the nun lightened. Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub read: "wa-la yastakhiffannaka," meaning: let them not provoke you, so that they overpower you and become more entitled to you than the believers.
